summary: Specifies how to put audio compressed with the ITU-T G.729.1 codec into Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) packets for live streaming over IP. It also registers the media type for the payload format.

plainLanguage.summary:
G.729.1 is a speech codec that can produce audio at any of twelve bit rates between 8 and 32 kbps, and it can switch between them while a call is running. This RFC defines how those compressed frames travel inside RTP packets.

Every packet starts with a one-byte header. Half of that byte says the highest bit rate the sender can handle, and half says what rate the frames in this packet use and how big they are. The maximum bit rate field lets a receiver ask the sender to use less bandwidth, without a separate negotiation message.

subtitle: How to put G.729.1 compressed speech into RTP packets, including a way to ask the other end to slow down.

tldr.problem: G.729.1 is a scalable wideband speech codec whose bit rate can change on the fly, but no payload format existed for carrying it over RTP, and no way existed for a receiver to tell the sender to use less bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP payload carries a one-octet header with a 4-bit MBS field advertising the highest bit rate the receiver can take and a 4-bit FT field giving the rate and frame size of the audio frames that follow.
tldr.outcome: The payload format lets a sender drop its bit rate without any signalling and lets a receiver ask the sender to do so with the MBS field. The RFC was later updated by RFC 5459.

facts.label: RTP clock rate
facts.value: 16 kHz, timestamp step of 320 per frame

today: RFC 4749 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, and it was updated by RFC 5459. The payload format it defines is still the way G.729.1 audio travels in RTP packets.

sections.title: What This RFC Specifies
sections.content:
The ITU-T recommendation G.729.1 is a scalable wideband extension of the recommendation G.729 audio codec. This document specifies the payload format for packetising G.729.1 encoded audio signals into the Real-time Transport Protocol. The payload format itself is described in Section 5, and a media type registration together with the details for using G.729.1 with SDP are given in Section 6.

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines three things: how compressed audio is laid out inside an RTP packet, how the media type for it is registered, and how a session description announces it.

sections.title: The G.729.1 Codec
sections.content:
G.729.1 is an 8 to 32 kbps scalable wideband, 50 to 7000 Hz, speech and audio coding algorithm that is interoperable with G.729, G.729 Annex A and G.729 Annex B. It provides a standardised solution for packetised voice applications that allows a smooth transition from narrowband to wideband telephony.

The services addressed are IP telephony and videoconferencing, either in enterprise corporate networks or in the mass market, such as Public Switched Telephone Network emulation over DSL or wireless access. Target devices can be IP phones or other VoIP handsets, home gateways, media gateways, IP Private Branch Exchange equipment, trunking equipment and voice messaging servers.

For all of those applications the scalability feature allows tuning the bit rate against the quality trade-off, possibly in a dynamic way during a session, taking into account service requirements and network transport constraints.

The G.729.1 coder produces an embedded bitstream structured in 12 layers, corresponding to 12 available bit rates between 8 and 32 kbps. The first layer, at 8 kbps, is the core layer and is bitstream compatible with the G.729 and G.729A coders. At 12 kbps a second layer improves the narrowband quality. Upper layers provide wideband audio between 14 and 32 kbps with a 2 kbps granularity, allowing graceful quality improvements. Only the core layer is mandatory for decoding understandable speech; the upper layers provide quality enhancement and wideband enlargement. The codec operates on 20 ms frames, and the default sampling rate is 16 kHz. Input and output at 8 kHz are also supported, at all bit rates.
sections.plainLanguage: The codec builds its output in layers. The bottom layer alone gives understandable narrowband speech; each layer above adds quality or bandwidth. A sender can add or drop layers at any moment and the receiver decodes what it gets.

sections.title: Embedded Bit Rates and the MBS Request
sections.content:
The embedded property of G.729.1 streams provides a mechanism to adjust bandwidth demand. At any time a sender can change its sending bit rate without external signalling, and the receiver will still be able to decode the frames properly. That may help to control congestion, since the bandwidth can be adjusted by selecting another bit rate.

The ability to adjust bandwidth may also help on a fixed bandwidth link dedicated to voice calls, for example in a residential or trunking gateway, where the system can change bit rates depending on the number of simultaneous calls. This only affects the sending bandwidth. To adjust the receiving bandwidth as well, the document introduces an in-band signalling request that asks the other party to change its own sending bit rate. That request is called MBS, for Maximum Bitrate Supported, and is described in Section 5.2.

MBS is only useful for two-way unicast G.729.1 traffic, because when A sends an in-band MBS to B to ask B to modify its sending bit rate, it concerns the stream from B to A. If there is no G.729.1 stream in the reverse direction, the MBS has no effect.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender can lower its own bit rate at any time without asking. Lowering the other end's bit rate takes a request, and that request travels inside the audio packets as a field called MBS.

sections.title: RTP Header Usage
sections.content:
The format of the RTP header is specified in RFC 3550, and this payload format uses the fields of that header consistently with that specification.

The RTP timestamp clock frequency is the same as the default sampling frequency, 16 kHz. G.729.1 can also operate with 8 kHz sampled input and output signals at all bit rates. That does not affect the bitstream, and the decoder does not need to know in advance the sampling rate of the original signal at the input of the encoder. Depending on the implementation and the acoustic capabilities of the devices, the encoder input and the decoder output can be configured at 8 kHz, but a 16 kHz RTP clock rate MUST always be used.

The duration of one frame is 20 ms, corresponding to 320 samples at 16 kHz, so the timestamp increases by 320 for each consecutive frame. The M bit MUST be set to zero in all packets.

The assignment of an RTP payload type for this packet format is outside the scope of the document. It is expected that the RTP profile under which this payload format is used will assign a payload type for this codec, or specify that the payload type is bound dynamically.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet carries a timestamp that counts 16,000 units per second. One audio frame lasts 20 ms, so the timestamp moves by 320 each frame. The marker bit is always zero, because every packet carries whole frames.

sections.title: The Payload Format
sections.content:
The complete payload consists of a payload header of 1 octet followed by zero or more consecutive audio frames at the same bit rate. The payload header has two fields: MBS, which is 4 bits, and FT, which is 4 bits.

The MBS field carries the maximum bit rate supported and indicates a maximum bit rate to the encoder at the site of the receiver of this payload. Its values run from 0 for 8 kbps through 11 for 32 kbps, with 12 to 14 reserved and the value 15 meaning NO_MBS. The MBS tells the other party the maximum bit rate one can receive, so the encoder MUST NOT exceed the sending rate indicated by the received MBS. Because of the embedded property of the coding scheme, the encoder can send frames at the MBS rate or any lower rate, and can change its bit rate at any time without previous notice as long as it does not exceed the MBS. The MBS is a codec bit rate; the actual network bit rate is higher and depends on the overhead of the underlying protocols. A received MBS value stays valid until the next MBS is received. If a payload with a reserved MBS value is received, the MBS MUST be ignored. The MBS field MUST be set to 15 for packets sent to a multicast group, and MUST be ignored on packets received from a multicast group. It MUST also be set to 15 in all packets when the actual MBS value is sent through non-RTP means.

The FT field gives the frame type of the frames in the packet. Its values run from 0 for 8 kbps and 20 octets through 11 for 32 kbps and 80 octets, with 12 to 14 reserved and the value 15 meaning NO_DATA. The value 15 indicates that there is no audio data in the payload. This MAY be used to update the MBS value when there is no audio frame to transmit, in which case the payload is reduced to the payload header. If a payload with a reserved FT value is received, the whole payload MUST be ignored.

Audio data in a payload contains one or more consecutive audio frames at the same bit rate, packed in order of time, oldest first. The size of one frame comes from the FT field, and the number of frames is inferred from the size of the audio data part: nb_frames = size_of_audio_data divided by size_of_one_frame. Only full frames are considered, so any remainder in the received payload MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet holds one byte of header followed by audio frames. The header says how fast the sender is going and how big each frame is. The receiver works out how many frames arrived by dividing the data length by the frame size, and drops any leftover bytes.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The media type is registered from the template in RFC 4288, following RFC 3555. The type name is audio, the subtype name is G7291, and there are no required parameters. The optional parameters are maxbitrate, the absolute maximum codec bit rate for the session in bits per second, whose permissible values are 8000, 12000, 14000, 16000, 18000, 20000, 22000, 24000, 26000, 28000, 30000 and 32000, with 32000 implied if the parameter is omitted; mbs, the current maximum codec bit rate supported as a receiver, with the same set of permissible values but constrained to be lower than or equal to maxbitrate, and set to the maxbitrate value if omitted; and ptime and maxptime, the recommended and maximum length of time in milliseconds that the media in a packet represents. The bit rates indicated by the FT and MBS fields in the RTP packets MUST NOT exceed maxbitrate.

For SDP, the media type goes in the m= line as the media name, the subtype goes in a=rtpmap as the encoding name with an RTP clock rate that MUST be 16000 for G.729.1, ptime and maxptime go in the matching attributes, and any remaining parameters go in a=fmtp as a semicolon separated list of parameter and value pairs.

Under the SDP offer-answer model, the offerer SHOULD announce G.729 support in its m=audio line with G.729.1 preferred, so that a G.729-only party can still take part. The maxbitrate parameter is bi-directional: if the offerer sets a value, the answerer MUST reply with a smaller or equal value, and the actual maximum for the session is the minimum. The mbs parameter is not symmetric; values in the offer and the answer are independent and reflect local constraints, and neither party MUST start sending frames at a bit rate higher than the other party's mbs. For sendonly streams the mbs parameter is useless and SHOULD NOT be used, while for recvonly streams it is the only way to communicate the MBS to the sender, since there is no RTP stream towards it. For multicast the mbs parameter MUST NOT be used, and maxbitrate becomes declarative and MUST NOT be negotiated. In declarative SDP, such as SAP and RTSP, the mbs parameter MUST NOT be used and maxbitrate is declarative.
sections.plainLanguage: The media type is audio/G7291, and a session description carries the rate limits as parameters. The session maximum is whichever side asks for less. The MBS value is per direction, so each side states its own limit, and it means nothing in multicast.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content:
Congestion control for RTP SHALL be used in accordance with RFC 3550 and any appropriate profile, for example RFC 3551. The embedded and variable bit rate capability of G.729.1 provides a mechanism that may help to control congestion.

The number of frames encapsulated in each RTP payload influences the overall bandwidth of the RTP stream, because of the header overhead. Packing more frames in each payload can reduce the number of packets sent and hence the header overhead, at the expense of increased delay and reduced error robustness.
sections.plainLanguage: Putting several frames in one packet saves the cost of repeated headers, but adds delay and makes a single lost packet cost more audio. The codec's variable rate gives another lever, since the sender can drop to a lower rate when the network is busy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RTP packets using this payload format are subject to the general security considerations discussed in the RTP specification and in any appropriate profile.

Because the format transports encoded speech and audio, the main security issues are confidentiality, integrity protection, and authentication of the speech and audio itself. The payload format itself has no built-in security mechanisms. Any suitable external mechanisms, such as SRTP, MAY be used.

The document also notes that this payload format and the G.729.1 encoding do not exhibit any significant non-uniformity in the receiver-end computational load, and so are unlikely to pose a denial-of-service threat due to the receipt of pathological datagrams.
sections.plainLanguage: The format carries no protection of its own. A separate mechanism such as SRTP is needed to keep the call contents private and to stop them being altered in transit.

fields.name: MBS
fields.desc: Maximum bit rate supported by the receiver of this payload. 0 to 11 map to 8 to 32 kbps, 15 means NO_MBS.

fields.name: FT
fields.desc: Frame type of the frames in this packet. 0 to 11 give the rate and frame size, 15 means NO_DATA.

viz.caption: FT VALUES: ENCODING RATE AND FRAME SIZE (RFC 4749)

items.title: A ceiling, not a setting
items.text: The sender may use the MBS rate or any lower rate, and may change rate at any time without notice.

items.title: Last one wins
items.text: A received MBS stays valid until the next MBS arrives, and a new value overrides the old one.

items.title: Reserved values
items.text: If a payload arrives with a reserved MBS value, that MBS is ignored.

items.title: No value in multicast
items.text: The MBS field is set to 15 in packets sent to a multicast group, and ignored on packets received from one.
